subject: English
description: Direct → indirect: tenses, pronouns, time expressions, modals

questions.stem: Convert: Ravi said, 'I am writing a letter.' to indirect speech:

options.option_text: Ravi said that I am writing a letter.
Ravi said that he was writing a letter.
Ravi said he is writing a letter then.
Ravi told that he wrote a letter then.

questions.explanation: Rules: (1) Pronoun shift — I → he (since Ravi is male, third-person). (2) Tense backshift — Present continuous (am writing) → Past continuous (was writing). (3) Reporting verb 'said' (no object) followed by 'that' clause. Distractor 1 — pronoun + tense not changed. Distractor 3 — tense not changed. Distractor 4 — wrong tense + 'told' needs an object.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert: She said, 'I will go to Delhi tomorrow.' to indirect speech:

options.option_text: She said she will go to Delhi tomorrow.
She said she would go to Delhi the next day.
She said that she would go Delhi tomorrow.
She said that she goes to Delhi next day.

questions.explanation: Two key shifts: (1) MODAL — 'will' → 'would' (backshift). (2) TIME — 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'. Standard time shifts: today → that day; tonight → that night; yesterday → the previous day; tomorrow → the next day; last week → the previous week; ago → before. Distractor 1 — no shifts. Distractor 3 — kept 'tomorrow'. Distractor 4 — wrong tense.

questions.stem: Convert (interrogative): He said to me, 'Where do you live?'

options.option_text: He asked me where do I live there.
He asked me where I lived (then/there).
He asked me where I do live there.
He asked me where did I lived there.

questions.explanation: Rules for QUESTIONS: (1) 'said to' → 'asked'. (2) Wh-question word kept. (3) Inverted Q-form (do you live) → STATEMENT order (you live → I lived after pronoun shift). (4) No question mark; ends with period. (5) Tense backshift — present (live) → past (lived). Distractor 1 — kept Q-order. Distractor 3 — kept 'do' helper. Distractor 4 — wrong tense (did + lived).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert (imperative): The teacher said to the students, 'Open your books.'

options.option_text: The teacher said students to open their books.
The teacher told the students to open their books.
The teacher said that students open their books.
The teacher asked open the books to them.

questions.explanation: Rules for IMPERATIVES (commands/requests): (1) 'said to' → 'told' / 'ordered' / 'requested' / 'asked' (depending on tone). (2) Imperative converted to TO-INFINITIVE — 'Open' → 'to open'. (3) Pronoun shift — 'your' → 'their'. (4) No 'that' clause for imperatives. Distractor 1 — missing 'to' (preposition). Distractor 3 — used 'that'-clause for imperative. Distractor 4 — order/wording wrong.

questions.stem: Convert: He said, 'The Sun rises in the East.' to indirect speech:

options.option_text: He said the Sun rose in the East then.
He said that the Sun rises in the East.
He said that the Sun was rising in East.
He said that Sun used to rise in East.

questions.explanation: EXCEPTION to backshift rule: UNIVERSAL TRUTHS / habitual facts / scientific truths keep their PRESENT TENSE in reported speech. 'Sun rises in East' is universally true → no backshift. Other examples: 'Honesty is the best policy', 'Two plus two is four', 'Earth revolves around the Sun'. Distractor 1 — incorrect backshift to past. Distractor 3 — wrong tense. Distractor 4 — wrong sense.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert (exclamatory): She said, 'What a beautiful sight!'

options.option_text: She said that beautiful sight existed.
She exclaimed that it was a very beautiful sight.
She said the sight was a beautiful sight.
She told that what a beautiful sight!

questions.explanation: EXCLAMATORY rules: (1) 'said' → 'exclaimed' / 'cried' / 'shouted' (carry the emotion). (2) Convert exclamation to STATEMENT — 'What a beautiful X!' → 'that it was a very beautiful X' (use 'very' / 'great' to carry the intensity). (3) Tense backshift. Distractor 1 — lost meaning. Distractor 3 — clumsy. Distractor 4 — kept exclamatory form.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert: 'Can you help me?' she said. The correct indirect form is:

options.option_text: She asked can I help her then.
She asked if I could help her.
She told me whether I help her.
She said me whether I would help.

questions.explanation: YES/NO QUESTION → introduced by IF or WHETHER. Modal CAN → COULD (backshift). Pronoun: you → I (if speaker is being addressed); me → her. Verb 'said' for question → 'asked'. Distractor 1 — kept Q-form. Distractor 3 — wrong tense (no backshift). Distractor 4 — 'said me' is wrong (should be 'told me' or 'said to me').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Mohan said, 'I visited the museum last year.' Which is the correct indirect form of this sentence?

options.option_text: Mohan said that he visited the museum last year.
Mohan said that he had visited the museum the previous year.
Mohan said that he has visited the museum the previous year.
Mohan said that he had visited the museum last year.

questions.explanation: B is correct: past simple ('visited') backshifts to past perfect ('had visited'), and 'last year' must change to 'the previous year'. Option A fails to backshift the tense. Option C wrongly uses present perfect 'has visited'. Option D backshifts correctly but leaves 'last year' unchanged — a common overlooked error.

questions.stem: She said, 'I have finished my homework.' The correct indirect speech form is:

options.option_text: She said that she has finished her homework.
She said that she had finished her homework.
She said that she finished her homework.
She said that she had been finishing her homework.

questions.explanation: B is correct: present perfect ('have finished') backshifts to past perfect ('had finished'). Option A incorrectly retains present perfect 'has finished'. Option C uses simple past — valid for backshifting present simple, not present perfect. Option D wrongly introduces past perfect continuous, implying an incomplete ongoing action, which distorts meaning.

questions.stem: Priya said, 'Let's go for a walk.' The correct indirect form of this suggestion is:

options.option_text: Priya said that let them go for a walk.
Priya suggested that they should go for a walk.
Priya told them that they go for a walk.
Priya ordered that they must go for a walk.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Let's...' expresses a suggestion, so the reporting verb must be 'suggested/proposed', not 'said' or 'told'. Structure becomes: suggested + that + subject + should + base verb. Option A retains 'let' inside the reported clause, which is grammatically wrong. Option C uses 'told' (wrong verb for suggestions) with no modal. Option D uses 'ordered', converting a mutual suggestion into a command and completely altering the speaker's intent.

questions.stem: The manager said to his team, 'You must submit the report today.' The correct indirect form is:

options.option_text: The manager told his team that they must submit the report today.
The manager told his team that they had to submit the report that day.
The manager said to his team they should submit the report today.
The manager told his team that you must submit the report that day.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'must' denoting external obligation changes to 'had to' in past reported speech; 'today' shifts to 'that day'; 'you' shifts to 'they'. Option A retains both 'must' and 'today' unchanged. Option C keeps 'today' and uses the non-standard 'said to his team' without 'that'. Option D correctly shifts 'today' to 'that day' but fails to change the pronoun 'you' to 'they' — a pronoun-shift oversight examiners frequently test.

questions.stem: The doctor said to the patient, 'Don't eat oily food.' Which option correctly reports this negative imperative?

options.option_text: The doctor said to the patient that he should not eat oily food.
The doctor advised the patient not to eat oily food.
The doctor told the patient that don't eat oily food.
The doctor commanded the patient to not eat oily food.

questions.explanation: B is correct: negative imperatives are reported as 'advised/told + object + not + to-infinitive'. 'Advised' suits the doctor's tone precisely. Option A uses a declarative 'that-clause' structure, which is non-standard for imperatives. Option C retains 'don't' inside the reported clause — the most frequent student error in negative imperative conversion. Option D uses 'commanded', implying authority and force, which misrepresents a doctor's advisory register.

questions.stem: She said to him, 'Did you lock the door before leaving?' Which option correctly converts this to indirect speech?

options.option_text: She asked him whether he locks the door before he left.
She asked him whether he had locked the door before leaving.
She said to him whether he had locked the door before leaving.
She questioned him if he had been locking the door before leaving.

questions.explanation: B is correct: a yes/no question in past simple ('Did...lock') backshifts to past perfect ('had locked'); auxiliary 'Did' is dropped; word order becomes declarative; 'whether/if' introduces the clause. Option A mixes tenses — 'locks' (present) inside the clause is inconsistent with the past reporting context. Option C uses 'said to him whether' — yes/no questions require reporting verb 'asked', not 'said to'. Option D uses past perfect continuous 'had been locking', implying an interrupted ongoing action, which misrepresents the simple completed act the original question tests.

questions.stem: He said, 'If I work hard, I will pass the exam.' The correct reported form of this conditional sentence is:

options.option_text: He said that if he works hard, he will pass the exam.
He said that if he worked hard, he would pass the exam.
He said that if he had worked hard, he would have passed the exam.
He said that if he worked hard, he shall pass the exam.

questions.explanation: B is correct: in a Type 1 (real/open) conditional reported in past tense, present simple 'work' → past simple 'worked', and 'will' → 'would'. The real-condition relationship is preserved. Option A makes no tense backshift at all — a basic error. Option C converts the sentence to a Type 3 (unreal past) conditional, changing 'If I work hard' (realistically possible) into a past hypothetical — a subtle but meaning-altering error that examiners prize. Option D wrongly uses 'shall' instead of 'would'; 'shall' is not the reported-speech equivalent of 'will' when the main clause is in the past.

questions.stem: Anita said to Rahul, "Your brother met me yesterday." Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: Anita told Rahul that his brother had met her the previous day.
Anita told Rahul that your brother had met her the previous day.
Anita told Rahul that his brother met her the next day.
Anita said Rahul that her brother had met him the previous day.

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'your' (Rahul's) shifts to 'his'; 'me' (Anita) shifts to 'her'; 'met' (simple past) back-shifts to 'had met' (past perfect); 'yesterday' shifts to 'the previous day'. Option B wrongly retains 'your' — the most common pronoun-change error. Option C fails to back-shift the tense and uses 'next day' instead of 'previous day'. Option D swaps pronouns wrongly, making 'her brother' and 'him' refer to incorrect antecedents.

questions.stem: He said, "I shall return the book tomorrow." Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: He said that he would return the book the following day.
He said that he will return the book the following day.
He said that he shall return the book the next day.
He said that he had returned the book the following day.

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'shall' used for the first person in direct speech back-shifts to 'would' in indirect speech; 'tomorrow' changes to 'the following day'. Option B uses 'will' instead of 'would' — a very common error where candidates apply second/third person rules. Option C retains 'shall' unchanged, ignoring the back-shift rule entirely. Option D uses past perfect 'had returned', falsely implying the action was already completed at the time of speaking.

questions.stem: Priya said to her friends, "Let us plan a trip to Goa next month." Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: Priya said to her friends that let them plan a trip to Goa the next month.
Priya suggested her friends that they should plan a trip to Goa the following month.
Priya suggested to her friends that they should plan a trip to Goa the next month.
Priya told her friends that they should plan a trip to Goa the following month.

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'Let us' signals a suggestion, reported as 'suggested + to + object + that + subject + should + verb'. Option A retains the direct form entirely without a proper reporting structure. Option B omits the necessary preposition 'to' — 'suggest' cannot take a direct object the way 'tell' or 'ask' can; it must be 'suggested to her friends'. Option D uses 'told...should', which implies a command or instruction rather than a mutual suggestion.

questions.stem: She said to me, "I have never visited the Red Fort." Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: She told me that she had never visited the Red Fort.
She told me that she never visited the Red Fort.
She said to me that she has never visited the Red Fort.
She told me that she never had visited the Red Fort before.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Present perfect 'have visited' back-shifts to past perfect 'had visited' in indirect speech. Option B uses simple past 'visited' — a frequent error that drops the perfect aspect, changing the nuance of the experience. Option C retains present perfect 'has never visited' without any back-shift. Option D wrongly splits the auxiliary, placing 'had' after 'never' and adding 'before', producing a non-standard and grammatically awkward construction.

questions.stem: The examiner said to the student, "Did you attempt all the questions?" Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: The examiner asked the student if he had attempted all the questions.
The examiner asked the student that did he attempt all the questions.
The examiner told the student whether he attempted all the questions.
The examiner asked the student whether he attempts all the questions.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Yes/no questions in indirect speech use 'if' or 'whether' as connector; the auxiliary 'Did' is dropped and the tense back-shifts: 'did attempt' → 'had attempted'. Option B wrongly retains the inverted question word order with 'that did he' — a common direct-to-indirect conversion error. Option C uses 'told' as the reporting verb, which is grammatically inappropriate for a question; also lacks back-shift. Option D retains present tense 'attempts' — no back-shift applied.

questions.stem: Suresh said, "If I get a transfer, I will move to Mumbai." Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: Suresh said that if he gets a transfer, he will move to Mumbai.
Suresh said that if he got a transfer, he would move to Mumbai.
Suresh said that if he had got a transfer, he would move to Mumbai.
Suresh said that if he would get a transfer, he would move to Mumbai.

questions.explanation: B is correct: A Type 1 conditional ('if + simple present, will + infinitive') back-shifts in indirect speech to 'if + simple past, would + infinitive': 'gets' → 'got', 'will move' → 'would move'. Option A retains the present tense and 'will' — no back-shift at all. Option C uses past perfect 'had got' in the if-clause — this is a subtle trap that incorrectly converts the sentence into a Type 3 (unreal/hypothetical past) conditional, changing the original meaning. Option D inserts 'would' in the if-clause, which is grammatically incorrect in any conditional type.

questions.stem: Maya said to her mother, "I have been waiting here for two hours and I am very tired." Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: Maya told her mother that she has been waiting there for two hours and she is tired.
Maya told her mother that she had been waiting there for two hours and she was very tired.
Maya said to her mother that I had been waiting here for two hours and I was very tired.
Maya told her mother she had been waiting there for two hours and had been very tired.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Multiple simultaneous shifts are required — present perfect continuous 'have been waiting' → past perfect continuous 'had been waiting'; simple present 'am very tired' → simple past 'was very tired'; 'here' → 'there'; 'I' → 'she'. Option A retains both present tenses with no back-shift and also omits 'very'. Option C retains first-person pronoun 'I' and proximity adverb 'here' — the classic error of neglecting pronoun and adverb changes. Option D upgrades 'was very tired' to 'had been very tired'; simple stative complements do not require past perfect — only the action verb 'waiting' needs perfect aspect.
